newsitem.title: CANADA: Loewen shares seen falling after bid axed.
newsitem.headline: Loewen shares seen falling after bid axed.

text.p: Funeral home operator The Loewen Group Inc savored a sweet victory Tuesday over hostile bidder Service Corp International, but analysts said the elation was likely to be tempered by a swift drop in Loewen's share price Wednesday.
Loewen rejoiced at news late Tuesday that Service, the industry giant, had withdrawn a US$2.9 billion bid for Loewen. Service said it feared recent actions by Loewen hurt its value.

But analysts and arbitragers said Loewen, which has survived several near-death experiences over the past year including a brush with bankrupcty, was likely to find itself under pressure again by Wednesday.
They predicted a fall of between five and 15 percent in Loewen's share price, which soared in September on first news of Service's bid. Service in October raised its offer to US$45 a share in stock.
Loewen stock closed Tuesday at US$40.875 in New York, up 12.5 cents.
"I would expect Loewen stock to move back. US$37 would probably be reasonable but it might go back as low as US$34," said one analyst who asked not to be identified.
One arbitrageur said he anticipated a drop of US$5 a share or so in Loewen's shares early Wednesday.
Service's announcement stunned investors. "This has caught everyone by surprise," said one trader.
Loewen too said it was caught off guard by the news but it welcomed Service's move. "We are obviously very pleased," a company spokesman said.

Analysts said that Loewen's stock should attract buying interest after an initial sell-off. The extent of the losses may be blunted because most investors who bought the stock purely for takeover interest have already sold their shares. Service had been waiting since October for regulatory approval of its offer and many traders had anticipated a long wait.

Loewen contended that Service was trying to buy it on the cheap and argued that the takeover would face challenges on antitrust grounds. The two companies were locked in an ongoing lawsuit over antitrust issues.

Meanwhile, Loewen kept up an aggressive acquisition campaign. It said last month that it had signed US$325 million in acquisitions since the Service deal was announced. It said the deals were a sign of industry confidence in Loewen.
Loewen and Service had competed ferociously against each other to make acquisitions in the rapidly consolidating funeral industry.

"Loewen made it clear its business was going very well. The shareholders sent the message to Service that at US$55 or US$60 (a share) they would start talking. At that price, SCI chickened out," one trader said.
